story_title: The Jug That Would Not Empty
place: A reed-roofed hut in the hills of Phrygia
summary: An old shepherd tells how a poor couple, Philemon and Baucis, welcomed two disguised strangers and found their wine jug would not empty. They asked only to stay together, and became an oak and a linden from one trunk.

teller.name: Stavros
teller.who: old shepherd on a hillside above the sea

listener: a hiker resting by the shepherd's fire on the hillside at dusk
hook: Which kind old couple served their last wine to two strangers, only to find the jug would not run dry, and what did they ask for in return?
context: Philemon and Baucis are a poor old couple of Phrygia who welcomed Zeus and Hermes in disguise; Ovid tells their story in the Metamorphoses.
source_tradition: Ancient Greece and Rome (Ovid, set in Phrygia)
source_note: Retold in original words from Ovid's Metamorphoses (public domain); no modern translation or retelling was followed.

image_brief: A dark hillside at dusk in ancient Greek Phrygia: a small campfire with a flask and a cloth of bread beside it, a low reed-roofed hut in the distance glowing with a lit doorway, two old trees growing from one trunk against a deep blue sky, dry grass and thyme. No faces, no text, no statues, no temples, no religious symbols.

script:
[[CHAPTER Welcome]]

Welcome to Fernwick Nights. Tonight we have The Jug That Would Not Empty, a lesser-known tale from the Greek myths, as told by Stavros, an old shepherd on a hillside above the sea. Get comfortable, and let the fire do its slow work.

[long pause]

[[CHAPTER A Poor House, a Full Table]]

Come closer to the fire, the ground is cold by now. There is a little wine in the flask, and bread in the cloth, and you are welcome to both. I mention the wine on purpose. Because tonight I want to tell you about a kind old couple who served their last wine to two strangers, only to find the jug would not run dry, and I want to tell you what they asked for in return. It is the best answer I know to the question of what to wish for.

[pause]

First, let me set the scene, so you can see where we are. We are sitting on the hillside above my sheep, on a flat stone still warm from the day. The fire is a small one, made of olive wood, and it crackles and pops and gives off a sweet smoke that smells a little like toasted nuts. My dog is asleep across my boots, heavy and warm. Down in the dark the bells of the flock clink now and then, softly, out of time with one another. And the wind moves through the dry grass with a long, easy rustle, like someone turning pages.

[pause]

Their names were Philemon and Baucis. You will not find them on many walls or in many schoolbooks. They are not heroes. They are not even kings. They were a poor old husband and wife who lived in a small hut in the hills of Phrygia, in the country we now call Turkey, and the Roman poet Ovid tells their story in his Metamorphoses. Ovid is the one who gathered up half the old tales and wrote them down in verse, so that we still have them.

[pause]

The hut had a roof of reeds and a wall of woven twigs plastered with mud. It was not much to look at. But they had married there when they were young, and grown old there together, and they never once talked about wanting a grander house. They were poor, and they knew it, and they carried it lightly, as you carry a good coat you have worn for forty years.

[long pause]

I knew a pair like them once, in the village below, a woman who baked flat bread in a clay oven and a man who mended shoes. Their doorstep was worn into a shallow dip by the feet of every visitor. The loaves were round and brown and still hot, and she would press one into your hands, split it open, and the steam would curl up smelling of wheat and sesame. Nobody ever left that doorstep hungry. I think of them whenever I tell this tale.

[long pause]

[[CHAPTER Two Strangers at the Door]]

Now, the old stories say that the gods sometimes walked among people, disguised as ordinary travelers, to see how they were treated. One evening Zeus and his son Hermes came down to this very country, dressed as tired wanderers with dust on their sandals. They knocked at a thousand doors. At every one they were turned away. Bolts slid shut. Dogs were called. Shutters closed. I always find that part hard to imagine, a whole land with its doors locked against two tired men.

[pause]

At last they came to the little hut with the reed roof. They had to bow their heads to go in through the low door. And the old couple welcomed them as if they were family. Philemon pushed forward a bench and spread a rough woolen blanket over it. Baucis raked the ashes aside to find a few warm coals, and fed them dry leaves and bark, and blew gently on them until a small flame stood up.

[pause]

She hung a pot over the fire. Philemon went out to the garden and came back with a cabbage, and she trimmed it, leaf by leaf. From the rafters she took down a piece of smoked bacon, hung there since last winter, and cut a modest slice. While the pot hummed on the fire, the old man filled a wooden trough with warm water so the guests could wash their feet. A mattress of soft river sedge was laid on the couch, with a faded cover that was kept for holidays.

[long pause]

Everything in that hut was simple, and everything had been used well. The floor was packed earth, swept smooth and cool under bare feet. The fire crackled low in a ring of stones. Smoke drifted up and found its own way out through the reeds, leaving a warm brown smell in the roof. A clay lamp burned on a ledge with a thread of oil, a small, steady, yellow light. And outside, the crickets were singing in the garden, and an owl called twice from the far side of the valley.

[long pause]

[[CHAPTER The Supper]]

The table had one short leg. It wobbled. So Baucis slipped a broken piece of pottery underneath, and wiped the top with a bunch of fresh mint, and the whole room smelled of green, cool leaves. Then she set out what they had. Olives, black and green. Cornelian cherries pickled in vinegar. Endive and radishes. Soft white cheese. Eggs baked gently in the warm ashes. All of it on plain clay dishes.

[pause]

There was wine, too, in an earthen jug, not much, mixed with water in a wooden bowl. Then came a second course: nuts and dried figs and dates, plums and small fragrant apples, and a bunch of purple grapes, and in the middle of the table a honeycomb, pale gold and dripping. The best thing, Ovid says, was the welcome, and the cheerful faces of the two old hosts, who were not trying to impress anybody.

[long pause]

I have eaten that meal, or something close to it. Cheese, black olives, bread, a fig, and a cup of thin red wine, on a plain table, with the evening coming in at the door. The cheese is salty and a little sour, the olives bitter and oily, the figs as soft as velvet and sweet as jam. The wine is cool in the clay cup. Everyone talks slowly. Nothing is hurried. The light turns from gold to rose to blue while the plates are still half full. I believe that is as near as anyone gets to what the old poet meant.

[long pause]

It was then that Philemon noticed something. Each time the bowl ran low, he refilled it from the jug. And each time he went back, the jug was full again. The wine poured, and the level in the jug never dropped. He nudged Baucis. Both of them went quiet. They realized, slowly, that their guests were more than they seemed.

[pause]

They trembled a little, and asked forgiveness for the poor meal. And Philemon remembered his goose, the one creature they owned, a noisy old bird that guarded the cottage. He decided to catch it for their guests. But the goose was quicker than the old man, and it ran, and ran, and finally took shelter in the folds of the strangers' cloaks. "Do not," said one of them, kindly. "Leave the goose alone."

[long pause]

[[CHAPTER The Hilltop]]

Then the strangers told them who they were. They led the old couple out of the hut and up a steep path to the top of a nearby hill. The two climbed slowly, leaning on their sticks, and the evening air was cool and smelled of thyme. At the top, Philemon and Baucis turned and looked down.

[pause]

The whole valley, the whole country of the unkind doors, had quietly vanished beneath still water. Like a shallow lake at dusk, silver and flat, with the last light lying on it. The only thing standing above the surface was their own small hut. And as they watched, the hut began to change. The reeds went gold. The walls turned to marble, the pale marble of the hills, and the roof shone like a crown. Columns rose where the posts had been.

[long pause]

"Ask what you like," said Zeus, "and you shall have it." The old couple whispered together for a moment, then Philemon spoke. They asked only to be allowed to look after the place, and to leave this world at the same hour. Neither of them wished to see the other's grave.

[long pause]

[[CHAPTER One Tree, Two Branches]]

Ovid says it was so. They tended the shining house for many years, and grew older and slower, and kept the habit of sitting side by side in the evening. One day, as they stood on the steps of the house, very old, they saw each other's skin begin to turn to bark. Leaves sprouted on their shoulders. They had time only to say goodbye, to say "farewell, my dear" to each other, and then the bark closed gently over their faces.

[pause]

Where they had stood there grew two trees from a single trunk, an oak and a linden. Shepherds in that country, so Ovid says, would still show visitors the pair, with their branches woven together, and hang small garlands on them. Ovid himself says he heard it from an old man who had seen them.

[long pause]

I like to think the leaves still touch in the wind. There is a hush in the hills tonight, and the fire is down to its last red coals. I do not know whether the story is true. But I know that the hut was small, and the table wobbled, and the wine never ran out, and that is a good deal more than most of us get.

[long pause]

[[SECOND]]

[[CHAPTER Once More, Slowly]]

Who served their last wine to two strangers, and found the jug would not empty? An old couple, Philemon and Baucis.

[pause]

Every door was shut against the travelers but theirs. They lit the small fire. They laid the table with olives, cheese and honey.

[long pause]

The jug stayed full. The strangers showed who they were. And the couple asked only to stay together.

[pause]

So they grew into two trees, an oak and a linden, from one trunk. Their leaves still touch in the wind.

[long pause]

So that is the tale of the jug that would not empty. The fire is low, the wine is yours, and the hill will keep you as long as you like. Good night.
